title: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (6 of 7)
hook: a ghost, a dog's curly tail, and why you can't fix the world
tomorrow: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (7 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: with your own work, worship. Offered work is careful work. Your line: offer the work. Did one task get the first-roti treatment? Day two hundred sixty-five.

A year of volunteering, donating, showing up for the cause, and the problem looks exactly the same. The shelter is still full. The inbox is still full. And a quiet voice asks: what's the point? Vivekananda took that question seriously. In his Karma Yoga lectures he answered it with a strange little story about a man, a ghost, and a dog's tail that would not stay straight. The chapter's title sounds almost rude: We Help Ourselves, Not the World.
screen: `THE PROBLEM LOOKS THE SAME.` → `WHAT'S THE POINT?` → `WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as Vivekananda tells it. A man wanted a ghost to do his work for him, and he got one. But there was a catch: the ghost had to be kept busy every minute, or it would kill him. The ghost finished every job in no time. Build a house: done. Clear a field: done. The man, terrified, ran to a wise teacher, who said: tell it to straighten a dog's curly tail. The ghost pulled the tail straight. Let go, and it curled back up. Pulled it again. Curled. That kept it busy. The world, Vivekananda said, is like that dog's tail. People keep pulling it straight. Let go, and it curls. So is helping pointless? No. That's the turn. When we help, he said, we're not fixing the world. The world will go on. We are the ones being changed. It's the helper who grows. So, he said, be grateful to the person you help. They gave you the chance. Then he adds the second half: work like a master, not a slave. A slave works for the reward, and is crushed when it doesn't come. A master works freely, because the work is worth doing. The Gita has a picture for it: the one who acts, offering the action and letting go of attachment, isn't stained by it, the way a lotus leaf sits in water and stays dry. The tail still curls. You keep straightening it anyway, and you stay dry.
screen: `A GHOST THAT MUST BE KEPT BUSY.` · `THE WORLD IS A DOG'S CURLY TAIL.` · `THE HELPER IS THE ONE WHO CHANGES.` · `A LOTUS LEAF IN THE WATER.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one thing you keep trying to fix that keeps curling back. A cause, a messy house, a relative who won't change. Breathe in, and feel how much you want the result. Breathe out, and set the result down beside you, just for now. Then picture yourself doing the next small piece anyway, not for the result, but because it's worth doing. See the lotus leaf: in the water, and dry. The bell holds the time.
Karma yoga deep-dive, part six. We help ourselves, not the world: the work changes the worker. Work like a master, not a slave, and stay dry like the lotus leaf.
Your line: offer the work. Today, help one person without checking whether it worked. And if you can, quietly thank them for letting you. Day two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: In seva, service offered freely, many Hindus aim to help without clinging to results or credit, often using the Gita's image of the lotus leaf that sits in water without getting wet.

match.prompt: the story and its point — tap the pairs.

myth: Vivekananda said helping others is pointless because the world won't change
he said helping is how the helper grows, and we should be grateful to the ones we help.
the Gita compares unattached action to a lotus leaf in water
Gita 5.10: offered action doesn't stain, as water doesn't wet the lotus leaf.
'work like a master, not a slave' means make others work for you
it means work freely, because the work is worth doing, not for the reward.

fork.setup: you're the man. the ghost has finished every job, and it will kill you if it's idle. what does the teacher tell you?
options: have it straighten a dog's curly tail.
give it a very big house to build.
fork.reveal: the curly tail: pulled straight, it curls back, forever. Vivekananda's picture of the world, and of work that never ends.

original.note: Sanskrit, Gita 5.10: 'like a lotus leaf by water' — untouched by what it sits in.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma yoga is about fixing the world through good works.
what it means: the work is worth doing, but its deepest effect is on the one who does it, freely and without clinging.

what a scholar hears: Vivekananda's 'we help ourselves, not the world' reframes service as spiritual discipline; the lotus-leaf image is Gita 5.10 (padmapatram ivāmbhasā), a common picture in Indian texts for being in the world without being stained by it.
